canonical_title: Other aspects of Transportation and Factors to consider

versions.title_at_revision: Other aspects of Transportation and Factors to consider
versions.text: K.1 Introduction This document provides guidance on the effects of transportation on Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS). In the context of this document, ‘UAS’ refers to the aircraft and all supporting systems that require transportation in order to support the aircraft. This document is designed to be generic so it can be applied to many different systems. However, aircrafts outside the weight range of 150kg to 20,000kg could potentially have unique transportation requirements so are outside the scope of this document. Transportation by land, sea or air exposes components to potentially damaging levels of vibration. Examples include the vibrations in propeller aircraft, an uneven ride from a truck driving off-road or passage over rough seas. Vibration levels can be severe, so should be taken into account when calculating component life. The transportation environment has to be correctly defined if the risk of component failure is to be fully understood. This document outlines one method of quantifying the transport environment. This is done by defining a usage profile (what transportation modes are used, how they are used and for how long) and attaching a vibration profile to each part of that usage profile. This allows a vibrations test to be defined which represents the entire transportation life of the UAS. The process described in this document is shown graphically in Figure 1 (in the red box). Since vibration can be a primary driver to the final design of the UAS or its packaging, the designer should be involved from the outset. Figure 1 – Vibration qualification and management process The purpose of this document is not to guide a particular design or suggest actual solutions but to aid the design process. This information should be used to drive the design of whatever system is to be Develop the requirements for the UAS. Design UAS following STANAG 4671 guidance where applicable. Identify transportation and usage requirements for the UAS. Source vibration data either from a standard or other suitable source Derive a vibration test which causes equivalent damage to transporting the UAS over its entire service life. The spectrum should be evaluated using a cumulative damage theory, such as Milner’s law, using the harshest vibration environment likely to be experienced for a duration long enough to account for all vibration environments. Qualification program validating the design process. UAS enters service and managed in accordance with National requirements. Evaluation of UAS usage, service life and logistics environment changes Understand significance of any changes with respect to original qualification. used to protect the UAS from vibration, be it a special container or inbuilt vibration isolation. This document is split into the following sections: K.2 The effects of vibration upon different materials and structures, K.3 Differences between the different transportation environments, K.4 Deriving transportation usage profiles, K.5 Deriving vibration profiles, K.6 Deriving test specifications from usage and vibration profiles, K.7 Performing a vibration test, K.8 Other transportation considerations which should be considered. It is important to note that transportation exposes equipment to a wide range of potentially damaging conditions. This document only focuses on the vibration environment. Other transportation factors which should be considered are discussed in section 8. K.2 The effects of vibration upon different materials and structures When subjected to vibration, part of a structure or internal components will typically deflect or move in some way. Such motion will generate a certain level of strain and over time such strain can be detrimental to structural integrity. Vibration can also cause damage or affect the functionality of electronics and mechanical systems either by causing component failure or disruption to sensors or systems. Each part of the UAS design can therefore be affected so vibration should be considered from the outset: Metals Metallic components or structures which are exposed to cyclic loading (e.g. vibration) can be susceptible to fatigue, leading to a reduction in strength or ultimately, failure. If vibration causes stresses due to flexing or differential loading then this could lead to crack initiation and propagation. The designer should be aware of how vibration energy will manifest itself in the structure and internal components. Section 5 outlines a method for quantifying damage to metallic structure through vibration. The effect of stresses on metallic structures (including electronic equipment with metal elements) is well understood so the comparative effect of vibration can be quantified and summed using classical fatigue theory. Miner’s law can be used to arrive at a vibration test with a level and duration with an equivalent level of damage to the entire transportation life. Composites Composites behave differently to metallic materials. Various modes of failure such as matrix cracking, delamination, fibre breakage, fibre kinking, wedge effect and inter-laminate shear failure could develop and lead to either initial or final failure. These modes are created as a result of application of multi-axial loads. The interaction between the above modes of failure is material and loading dependent. Matrix cracking in an isolated ply leads to failure while matrix cracking in a multi-directional laminate usually takes place at small load amplitudes and does not immediately lead to final failure. In the absence of experimental and test data, matrix damage introduced by vibration could be modelled using an interactive failure criterion such as Tsai-Hill. Multiple matrix cracking could develop into delamination and this could lead to deteriorating effects on the integrity of the composite structure. Miner’s law may be used for composites in a manner similar to that of metals in order to assess the vibrational effects on the integrity of the structures. The value of exponent used for Miner’s law calculations depends upon a number of parameters such as the composite lay-up, loading direction and environmental factors as well as the type of material used. An appropriate exponent should selected by a composites specialist. In addition, composites are particularly sensitive to temperature change and moisture up-take as well as to damage from impacts. Care should be exercised to avoid detrimental effects such as these in the presence of vibration if they could increase the risk of matrix damage. Systems Any equipment which could suffer reduced reliability through movement, accelerations or vibration is at risk due through transportation. Any components (such as circuit boards or other electronic components) constructed with metal can be damaged by fatigue if they are allowed to move. Most components of this type can be assessed using the same theory as any metal component, such as the technique specified within section 5. Other systems, such as mechanical linkages, hydraulics and sensors which make use of moving parts can also be affected. Qualifying such components depends on their usage and any prior knowledge about how susceptible they are to vibration. Any final qualification tests should prove that there is no long term reliability issue. K.3 Differences between the various transportation environments Each type of transportation has its own vibration characteristics and therefore contributes differently to the total vibration spectrum; a summary of each is presented below. A greater description of these environments is found in Def Stan 00-35 Part 5 Section 2. Propeller aircraft (for example C-130). Vibrations originate from the engines, mechanical components and pulses of air pressure (caused by the rotating propeller blades) acting against the fuselage and, possibly, from flow interaction with the empennage. The pressure waves occur at specific frequencies (e.g. blade passing frequency) and so can excite objects with appropriate resonant frequencies. Airflow past the fuselage can also produce vibration. The exposure to vibration depends on the position within the aircraft, for example, there is a significant increase in vibration when in line with the propellers or in close proximity to the fuselage wall. Jet aircraft (for example C-17). Vibrations originate from rotating engine components and airflow past the fuselage. The magnitude of these and the risk of damage depend on the position within the aircraft but in general, compared to propeller aircraft, jet aircraft offer a benign transport environment. Helicopters. Vibrations originate from the rotor blades and associated rotating mechanical components. Pressure waves caused by the rotating blades acting against the fuselage are also a significant factor. The magnitude of these depends heavily on the position within the aircraft. Vibration levels can be high in comparison with other forms of air transportation. Underslung. Loads slung beneath a helicopter are generally isolated from vibrations generated by the aircraft. Aerodynamic forces such as turbulence can vibrate a slung load but it is likely to be benign. Rail. Vibrations are generally limited to regular low level inputs due to movement along the tracks. Rail travel is generally benign when compared to other transport modes. The rail wagon size and type, rail quality and coupling method all affect the level of vibration experienced. Sea. Ship vibrations are typically generated from the propulsion system and other mechanical systems. The level of vibration seen is therefore dependent on the distance between the payload and the mechanical system in question. Rough seas can create large motions of the ship and the action of waves against the hull can send vibrations throughout the structure. Ship motion (governed by the sea state) can excite objects with low natural frequencies. Given the potential length of sea journeys such long exposure could be damaging to susceptible structures. Wheeled Vehicles. Vibrations are generated from mechanical systems and undulations in the terrain not filtered out by the vehicle’s suspension. The quality of the ride is therefore dependent on a number of variables which need to be taken into account before deriving a vibration test schedule: Vehicle type – there is a wide range of vehicles available for logistics efforts depending on the size and weight of the payload. Each vehicle type has different ride characteristics and proficiency at isolating the load area from undulating terrain. The load state of the vehicle – logistics vehicle suspension is designed for a certain payload. If a vehicle is very lightly loaded the suspension will not be operating within an optimal range and the ride will suffer. This can significantly affect the ride quality. Where the payload is positioned will affect the ride quality. Generally, ride quality is worst above axles. The terrain type. A wide range of potential terrains exist which can produce very different vibration environments. Terrain is the main variable to consider, as some off-road terrains can be severe and unpredictable. Tracked vehicles. The vibration environment associated with tracked vehicles is potentially the most severe of any transport option. The large powerplants generate a lot of noise and vibration while the stiff body and suspension allows easy transmission throughout the structure. Another significant factor is track patter, a repetitive action caused by each section in the vehicle track impacting the ground. The repetitive nature of this load establishes itself as a vibration, the frequency and magnitude of which is dependent on the vehicle’s speed, track design and condition and the type of terrain being traversed. A lot of transport environments are difficult to quantify given the variables, but conservative vibration spectra are provided within Def Stan 00-35 Part 3. These are discussed in section 5 of this document, along with how to generate alternatives which could be more representative. K.4 How to derive a transportation usage and transportation profile The way in which a UAS will be transported operationally needs to be recognised. This can be detailed within a usage and transportation profile (simply referred to as a usage profile in this document) which should contain details of every type of journey likely to be carried out. Each journey should be sufficiently detailed so that a vibration spectrum can be defined and attached to it. Typically, the more remote the location that the UAS is launched/recovered from, the more complex the usage profile will be. In order to define a usage profile, a number of assumptions need to be made regarding the operational use of the UAS and the logistics effort required to support it. There are different potential ways in which this can be defined, but a suggested process is detailed in Figure 2. It will be necessary to repeat this process for each element of the UAS (i.e. any piece of equipment which will be transported). Some equipment may not travel directly with the UAS so will have different transportation requirements. Once the entire transportation usage profile of the UAS has been derived (i.e. until the out of service date) the total mileage for each transport medium/condition can be calculated. It is important to use the correct vibration profile for each transportation type. Depending on the total payload, the vibration environment can change. The overall size and weight will determine what carriage options are available and what sort of vibration levels will be experienced by the UAS within its container (if applicable). The use of real trials data is always recommended. This is discussed in section 5. Figure 2 – Suggested process for the derivation of a transportation usage profile K.5 How to derive vibration profiles Defence Standard 00-35 Part 3 (Chapter 2 Annex A) provides default vibration profiles for most possible transportation modes. The Defence Standard advises that these should be used only if no specific vibration data is available. The use of real data is always recommended so the environment can be defined as accurately as possible. Vibration data is collected during trials over a preset frequency range appropriate to the test – for example a typical range for a road vehicle would be 0-2000Hz. Data collected from the accelerometers is typically displayed in the form of power spectral density (PSD) plots which expresses how the power density (e.g. power per Hz) of an energy source is distributed across a given frequency range. This usually allows for easy identification of any resonance spikes or areas with particularly high vibration levels, provided that these have not been disguised by band averaging. When sufficient vibration data has been gathered, it is possible to derive a vibration test which has an equivalent damage to the transportation life of the UAS. Once the transportation life has been established, and a vibration profile has been derived for each mode within that life, a single test can be derived. The process is described within Defence Standard 00-35 (Part 5, chapter 6-01 Annex A) in greater detail but the concept is to use the worst vibration environment (such as off-road vehicle running) and proportionally scale the time spent testing at that environment so it reflects the same damage caused by all transportation modes, the majority of which are likely to be far more benign. This method allows for a significant drop in the test duration while at the same time avoiding exposing the UAS to an accelerated test regime which may create unrepresentative damage and ultimately an over-engineered design. Miner’s law for fatigue damage is used as the basis for the scaling of testing time with the equation below: N S S T T        2 1 1 2 Where: S1 = Vibration level attributed to a particular transport mode. This can be expressed as the grms (root mean square acceleration) figure derived from a particular PSD plot. S2 = Worst case vibration level, associated with the harshest likely mode of transportation. Depending on the final test method this level should have an additional factor added to it to allow for the limited range typically associated with vibration rig equipment. This is discussed in section 7. T1 = Length of time spent on a particular transportation type. T2 = Time required at S2 level to produce equivalent damage to T1 at the S1 energy level. N = Slope of the S-N curve for the predominant structural feature associated with the UAS. Once T2 has been calculated for each transport condition, the total test duration can calculated. It is possible to adjust the resultant test duration for another/different vibration energy by using the same equation again, typically if the test duration is undesirably long. The duration can be reduced if a commensurate increase in test level can be tolerated. Sacrifices may be made in terms of test accuracy if this is taken too far so care should be taken in doing this and a vibration specialist consulted. The tests suggested in this document are an appropriate way of representing exposure to levels of vibration seen during transportation. While Miner’s law is used to represent vibration in terms of equivalent fatigue damage, it should be recognised that the method is only statistically reliable if variations in nominally identical structures are taken into account using a material scatter factor. In addition to this, potential future changes to the usage profile should be allowed for. If it changes so that a greater proportion of a harsher transportation mode is used then the qualification test identified could be inadequate. This could be dealt with by applying a suitable safety factor, to cover this uncertainty. The acceleration PSD plot can be used to derive the grms, found by calculating the area under the line and then taking the square root. The grms is an indication of the average severity of a particular vibration trace. It is this value which is used in section 6 of this document to derive an equivalent damage vibration test, representative of the entire transportation life. This method should not be the only way of considering the vibration environment. As grms represents vibration power in an average form, details of peaks in vibration levels and the overall shape of the profile are lost. Peaks/spikes in the levels could represent resonances which could be significant to the design of the UAS or its container. A certain amount of engineering judgement is required to identify how significant peaks and troughs in PSD plots are with respect to the data as a whole and whether the frequency at which the peak exists could affect the UA structurally. A vibration specialist should be consulted. K.6 How to derive a test specification from usage and vibration profiles Once the duration and vibration level has been derived, the shape of the test profile has to be established. This can be done by using the suggested profiles found in Defence Standard 00-35 (factored upwards/downwards accordingly to represent the required grms level S2). This can then be tailored as required by adding any peaks or spikes from any trials data. The result of this will be a profile which includes all the worst features of the trials data and a grms level appropriate to the entire transportation life. Different transportation modes (land, sea etc.) will have naturally different shape profiles. Engineering judgement should be used to determine how important it is to represent all transportation modes. For example, typically rail vibration profiles are typically more benign than that of road vehicles or propeller aircraft. In this case, depending on how much time is spent transporting the UAS on trains, the rail vibration profile may be ignored. An example of a way to work out T2 and S2 is shown in Table 1. There are many possible iterations of this process, and judgement should be used to derive a method which fully reflects the variables. Many vibration profiles will be unique to each UAS, as the size and weight of a payload can affect where and how it is carried, and the quality of ride it receives .Type of Transportation S1 T1 T2 Each transportation mode broken down by speed, vehicle type, terrain etc. grms level recorded for each given transportation type. ↓ S2 = Highest S1 value, with appropriate safety factors added (see sections 5 & 7). The final test will be carried out at this level. Actual length of time spent in using that transportation mode according to the usage profile, per average transport hour. Length of time required at S2 levels to represent this part of the usage profile. ↓ Sum T2 values to calculate the duration of test which has an equivalent damage to the transportation life of the UAS. Table 1 – Example method of calculating equivalent damage K.7 Performing a vibration test Careful consideration should be made concerning how any resultant vibration test is conducted. The payload should be positioned, supported and secured in the same fashion as when in used in service so the transfer of vibration loads is as representative as possible. Any modelling carried out should be subject to the same intentions. There are three approaches which can provide confidence in a design: Modelling Computer modelling creates a complete picture of stresses in the UAS without the need for a complex expensive trial. However, in order to have confidence in the results, some practical testing will be required to substantiate the results. Reliability of the design and practicalities surrounding transportation cannot be evaluated with a purely analytical approach. Vibration rig test Trials on a vibration rig are repeatable and controllable, with few variables and data collection is less complex than on field trials. However, they can be expensive and time consuming to set up before a realistic environment is created. Vibration rigs typically have movement limitations (for example maximum acceleration or displacement limits) which do not exist on field trials. An extra factor may be required to account for this. Representative field trial A representative method is to instrument a UAS and transport it as it would be operationally and assess whether if this causes damage. This type of qualification can also be used to test reliability and practicality of operation. However, it can lack repeatability due to the amount of variables involved. Defence Standard 00-35 part 3 chapter 2-14 outlines a procedure for running a test track trial. Any trial should, as far as is practicable, reflect the transportation vehicle defined in the usage profile. There are further drawbacks to a physical trial. It is difficult to represent the entire transportation life as it is harder to control the environment accurately. They are expensive and can be much more time consuming to carry out. K.8 Other aspects of transportation and factors to consider There are many aspects of transportation which can reduce the life or functionality of a system which fall outside the remit of this document. Such factors include: Shock Shock (transient) loads are associated with independent events such as an aircraft landing, a train shunting impact or a vehicle traversing a pot hole. Def Stan 00-35 part 5 chapter 2 discusses what shock loading is associated with transportation. Shocks can be damaging if they have sufficient acceleration and duration. They can be harder to quantify and predict if from an unexpected action (such as a handling error) but can be taken into account if only from a conservative stance. Shock loading can be monitored in service by the installation of a g exceedance meter of some form. This can indicate if the airframe/container has been exposed to an undesirable pulse. Consideration will have to be given to the threshold level chosen, where it is measured and how/with what periodicity the data is collected and recorded. Load restraint This document assumes that an adequate restraint scheme is used at all times. Unrestrained items are potentially subjected to far higher levels of vibration than those firmly secured to the vehicle in question, due to moving around and coming into contact with other objects. Def-Stan 00-3 details methods of restraining cargo when transported on land, rail and sea or in the air. There should be negligible movement between the vehicle and the load (except movement due to anti-vibration mounts) as this could amplify any vibration. The load restraint scheme should be capable of firmly retaining all elements of the load under all reasonably likely carriage manoeuvres. Logistics control The mechanics and practicalities of the logistics effort should be considered. If UAS are to be mated with a specific container for any reason (such as shock monitoring) consideration should be given to how maintenance and repair tasks are to be carried out – how will parts requiring maintenance or repair be moved around? If the normal container is used will this prevent the rest of the UAS being used for operations and will this be efficient for smaller parts? How will the remainder be stored in the interim? Environmental Def-Stan 00-35 (part 4) discusses the environmental considerations. Temperature, moisture, ice, sand and dirt etc. can all have a detrimental effect on the integrity and performance of a UAS. The packaging/container used for transport should protect the UAS as far as is required. Handling Any transfer of equipment into/out of transportation containers, or container transfers between logistics vehicles will involve lifting or handling. The way that each component is supported during this process should be considered as well as the repercussions and risk of handling errors. Special care has to be taken to protect composite structures from impact during handling. Storage The UAS may be stored in containers for a long period of time during a ship transit or between deployments. There should be no detrimental effects of long term storage. Environmental considerations are particularly pertinent due to the length of time that the UAS/container could be stored. Storage conditions designed to minimise the environmental risk to the UAS should be provided. Reliability Moving a UAS presents other challenges which may affect the functionality of the UAS or its container over time. The reliability of components or mechanisms is related to the harshness of the environment in which they are operated and the frequency of their operation. Items such as hinges, door seals, foam padding, bolted joints etc. are susceptible to wear and degradation. It would be expected that the design should not suffer from early failure, which can be proven to a certain extent by trials similar in nature to those used to confirm resistance to vibration. Longer term durability should be dealt with by a comprehensive maintenance regime.
